title: progressive-surface-ia-playbook-wip
body:
Purpose

This note collects heuristics, low-fi wireframe descriptions, and a pragmatic migration backlog for a progressive surface approach to the Console navigation and IA. The goal is to make the sidebar and routing predictable for power users while enabling a lightweight on-ramp for new users and feature teams. Focus is on: discoverability, task continuity, permission-aware surfaces, and minimizing churn for existing routes.

Background / constraints
- Console currently has ~35 top-level routes; users report cognitive load, long vertical nav, and duplicated entry points (e.g., model pages accessible from Catalog + Deployments).
- Product needs: support canary rollouts, per-route feature flags, and per-team quick links.
- Tech constraints: microfrontends experiment in progress (teams may deploy self-contained route bundles), routing layer is React Router v6 with a central route registry.
- UX constraints: must preserve deep links and bookmarks used by customers and support teams (customer links are embedded in Support docs).

High-level design principles
1) Progressive surface: show a minimal stable set of primary tasks (3–6) and reveal secondary surfaces in context or as expanding groups.
2) Route contracts: every route must declare: intention (task), canary flag, required permissions, breadcrumb hints, and canonical deep link (for bookmarks).
3) Permission-aware modularity: hide or collapse surfaces entirely for orgs without entitlement; do not reorder primary surfaces based on permissions (to avoid broken mental models).
4) Shortcut-first power tools: keyboard jump bar, pinned routes, and quick-actions to keep frequent flows 1–2 clicks.
5) Migration minimalism: change navigation names/paths only when necessary; provide transparent redirects + telemetry mapping for 90 days.

Proposed navigation anatomy
- Primary rail (left): persistent icons + short labels. Primary items are stable: Explore (search/command bar), Projects, Serving (live endpoints), Models (catalog), Monitor (observability), Billing.
- Secondary surface (collapsible): contextual groups under each primary tile. Example: Models -> [Catalog, Versions, Quantization Profiles, Benchmarks]. Collapsed by default for small viewports.
- Shortcuts ribbon (top of rail): pinned quicklinks (user-configurable, org-APIs), recent resources, and a single-click New... menu.
- Floating action + contextual onboarding: a small contextual FAB appears in empty states for first-time flows (e.g., "Create a Model Serving"), with mirrored deep link for support docs.

Routing and deep link rules
- Each route must implement a route contract file (route metadata) consisting of: route_id, canonical_path, alternate_paths (legacy), permission_tags, telemetry_key, and fallback_route. These are textual contract entries stored in central registry (not necessarily code — can be YAML/JSON files checked into the route registry repo).
- Backward compatibility: for any changed canonical_path, create 301-style client redirect and log usage to JIRA-PRIORITY-7689 mapping table. Keep redirects for >= 90 days, then evaluate.
- Route canonicalization: prefer resource-id-first paths for deep links: /models/{model_id}/versions/{version_id}/config instead of query heavy equivalents. Benefits: easier sharing, clearer breadcrumbs, and router-friendly caching.

Wireframe writeups (textual)
- Compact mode (default for wide screens): 56px left rail, icons + 1-line label on hover; primary tiles show badges (errors/warnings) and dot presence for live activity. Secondary groups slide out as a panel anchored to the tile (not the main content), allowing context without re-routing the primary content.
- Expanded mode (power users): 240px left rail with labeled groups, keyboard shortcut Ctrl+G toggles. Group headers are collapsible; active route group highlights the active child (breadcrumb visible).
- Mobile: bottom bar with 4 primary shortcuts and a global search command center. Deep linking behavior should open the console with the correct route anchor in the mobile shell.

Examples of specific route decisions
- "Serving" group: canonical path -> /serving. Subroutes: /serving/endpoints, /serving/capacity, /serving/rollouts. Deprecated legacy route /deploy should redirect to /serving/endpoints with telemetry tag old-deploy-link.
- "Models" group: merge Catalog + Model Library entry points into a single Catalog landing page with facet filters; keep /models/{id} stable. Add a shallow redirect from /catalog to /models to preserve external links.

Migration approach and rollout plan
Phase 0: Route registry + contracts (2 wks)
- Create route metadata files for top 50 routes. Add CI lint rule to validate required fields. Owner: eng-platform.
- Deliverable: registry PR; lightweight Confluence index.

Phase 1: Minimal surface + redirects (4 wks)
- Deploy compact rail implementation behind feature flag alpha-compact-rail. Implement redirects for renamed canonical paths; enable telemetry mapping. QA with solutions-engineering using saved bookmarks.
- Deliverable: alpha rollout to 10 internal orgs.

Phase 2: Secondary groups + pinned shortcuts (3 wks)
- Add collapsible groups and shortcuts ribbon; build personalization storage for pinned routes. Ship keyboard jump bar enhancements.

Phase 3: Power-user expansion & telemetry-driven tweaks (ongoing)
- After 30 days of telemetry, adjust primary items if usage < 2% for any item; carefully annotate changes in release notes.

Backlog grooming notes (stories, rough sizing, priority)
- CON-101: Implement route metadata registry and validator. (2 wks, L) [priority: high, owner: eng-platform]
- CON-102: Compact left rail skeleton + CSS var tokens. (1 wk, M) [priority: high, owner: frontend]
- CON-103: Redirect middleware & telemetry mapping table. (1 wk, M) [priority: high, owner: infra]
- CON-104: Shortcuts ribbon + pin API (server + client). (2 wks, M) [priority: med, owner: product-console]
- CON-105: Collapsible secondary groups panel UX + animation spec. (1 wk, S) [priority: med, owner: design]
- CON-106: Keyboard jump bar discovery improvements (visual hints the first session). (1 wk, S) [priority: low, owner: dx]

Acceptance criteria (sample)
- No preserved deep links break: top 50 external links must redirect to valid pages (automated smoke test).
- Top-3 tasks for each user persona reachable in <= 2 clicks from default rail.
- Permission-hidden surfaces must not change primary item ordering for user.

Open questions / trade-offs
- Should the primary tiles be re-orderable by users? (Pros: personalization. Cons: support overhead for docs/bookmarks.) Recommendation: allow per-user pin ordering only in the shortcuts ribbon, not the primary rail.
- How aggressive should we be in collapsing low-usage routes? Telemetry threshold proposal: <1% global usage for 60 days -> soft-deprecate. Need legal/enterprise opt-in signal for removal.
- Microfrontends: if teams ship route bundles that include their own nav, how to avoid double-nav? Proposal: standardize a topbar hook and provide a nav shim library for teams to consume.

Design notes & microcopy leanings
- Keep primary labels verb-first where possible ("Monitor" vs "Observability") to emphasize action.
- Hover state microcopy for collapsed rail: show short task hint + keyboard shortcut if available.
- Empty state CTAs must include support link + copy of deep link to copy/paste when needed.

Next steps (immediate)
- Validate list of top 50 routes with product managers and solutions-eng (due: 2025-02-17). Tag owners on the registry.
- Kick off CON-101 story and open route registry PR (owner: eng-platform).
- Schedule design review for the compact vs expanded states with SRE + DX (target: 2025-02-24).

Notes to self / scratchpad (informal)
- Quick test idea: A/B test condensed rail vs full rail on new users only; measure TTI for first task and support ticket rate.
- Keep an eye on customer docs referencing /deploy links — FYI thread in slack #solutions-cs.
- Link to earlier nav audit: CONFLUENCE-12345 (contains heatmaps and click funnels).

Footer
- Drafted by Riley Patel — please add inline comments. This is intentionally pragmatic: aim for incremental rollout with telemetry guardrails.
